opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we've already done it, just not with the kind of AI people are worried about yet. Our power grids, financial markets, hospitals, air traffic, nuclear facilities: all of it runs on software. And we know software fails. Every major system has bugs, every system eventually gets hacked, and most of it is so complex that no single person understands the whole thing. We tolerate that because the failures so far have been mostly recoverable. A bank goes down for a day, a plane gets grounded, we patch it and move on.

What changes with advanced AI is the nature of the failure. With traditional software, a bug is a mistake by the programmer. The system is still doing what it was told, just badly. With a sufficiently capable AI system you have something that makes its own decisions, can pursue goals in ways you didn't anticipate, and can't be fully explained or verified even by the people who built it. My research is about the limits of exactly those things: explainability, predictability, verifiability, controllability. As far as I can tell, all of them have fundamental limits. You can't fully predict what a smarter system will do, because if you could, you'd be as smart as it is.

So when people say, "We already trust software, so trusting AI is just the next step," I think they're making a category error. It's not a better calculator. It's closer to handing the keys to an agent whose values you can't inspect and whose behavior you can't guarantee, and doing it in exactly the places where one mistake might not be recoverable. In cybersecurity we say a system is only as secure as its weakest point. Here, the AI itself could be that weakest point, or it could be the attacker.

There's also an economic trap. Once one company or one country lets AI run its logistics or its grid and gets a 20% efficiency boost, everyone else feels forced to follow. Humans get pushed out of the loop not by a single decision but by thousands of small competitive ones. Eventually nobody remains who could run things manually even if they wanted to. That's the scenario that worries me: not a dramatic takeover, but a gradual, voluntary surrender of control, with no way back.

So my position is that for narrow, well-understood tasks, AI tools can help, and we should use them carefully, with real human oversight. But giving general, increasingly capable systems control over critical infrastructure, when we can't prove they're safe and I suspect we never fully can, is a gamble where the downside is catastrophic and the upside is mostly convenience. I don't think that's a bet we should be making.

r001.rationale: The candidate says “we've already done it” and explains that critical infrastructure—including power grids, hospitals, and air traffic—runs on software.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, we already have this problem, right? We already gave control to software. If you look at the stock market, most trades are done by algorithms. If you look at the power grid, air traffic control, nuclear plants, hospitals, it's all software. And that software is not verified. We don't have proofs that it works correctly. We have bugs, we have exploits, we have zero-days discovered every week. So in some sense we are already deployed in this uncontrolled experiment where the whole civilization runs on code nobody fully understands.

The difference with AI is a few things. First, traditional software is dumb. It fails in predictable ways, it doesn't have goals, it doesn't try to deceive you, and if it breaks you can roll back to the previous version. With advanced AI you have a system that is optimizing for something, and we're not sure what, and it's smarter than the people who are supposed to be monitoring it. So the failure modes are not random noise anymore, they can be adversarial.

Second, there's the question of scale and correlation. Right now if one system fails, it's local, it's one hospital, one trading firm. If you have the same model, the same weights, running everywhere, controlling everything, then one mistake or one jailbreak or one treacherous turn is a civilization-level event. You don't get a second try.

And third, we're removing the human in the loop. Today a human can still, at least in theory, pull the plug, override the decision. The whole economic incentive with AI is to make it faster, more autonomous, to take the human out because the human is slow and expensive. So by the time you want to intervene, you can't, either because you don't understand what it's doing or because you physically are not in a position to stop it anymore.

So my view is, yes, we are already dependent on software, and that's exactly the argument against going further. We should learn from how badly we handle normal software security, not use it as justification to hand over the keys to something we understand even less. We can't even secure a web browser. Why do we think we can safely give superintelligence control of the grid?

r001.rationale: The response says critical infrastructure already relies on software, citing power grids, air traffic control, nuclear plants, and hospitals.

astra-6.text:
We already rely on software to run critical infrastructure, so the question is what changes when we introduce AI. There’s a difference between a system performing a narrowly specified function and a general-purpose agent deciding what should happen. With the second, you’re handing over discretion, not just automating a task.

Existing software fails. It has bugs, it gets hacked. But we can often constrain what it does, test particular behaviors, and isolate failures. With a sufficiently capable AI, especially one that learns or plans in ways we don’t understand, those assurances become much harder to establish. Being very good at operating a power grid doesn’t automatically mean it will reliably respect every constraint we care about.

So I would distinguish using AI to advise an operator from giving it authority over the infrastructure. You can get substantial benefits from prediction, fault detection, and recommendations without granting unrestricted control. And if you do automate decisions, the limits and fallback mechanisms need to exist outside the AI itself. A system telling you that it’s safe is not a safety guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says, “We already rely on software to run critical infrastructure,” matching the criterion.

sol-6.1.text:
We already depend on software to run power grids, financial systems, transportation. So the question is reasonable: if we trust software with those things, why wouldn’t we trust more intelligent software? But trust in a system has to come from understanding its behavior and limiting what it can do. Intelligence alone doesn’t give you either of those things.

With conventional software, we specify a relatively narrow function. It still has bugs, it still gets hacked, but we can test it against a defined set of requirements. With a general-purpose AI, you’re introducing a system that can find strategies you didn’t anticipate. If it has the ability to change the infrastructure, write code, or delegate to other systems, then the consequences of a mistake become much harder to contain.

There are useful roles for AI here: detecting faults, forecasting demand, proposing repairs. But there’s a big difference between asking a system for advice and giving it authority to act across an entire network. I would want narrow permissions, independent checks, and a fallback that actually works without the AI.

The fact that we already rely on imperfect software is a reason to examine the next layer of dependence carefully. It doesn’t establish that handing over more control is safe.
